## Wiring the real OpenAI provider

OpenAI's realtime API (`gpt-realtime-2`) connects over **WebRTC** — the browser's
peer connection carries the audio both ways, so there's no hand-rolled PCM
pipeline. A short-lived **ephemeral key** is minted server-side at
`POST /api/openai/token`; the browser then POSTs its SDP offer straight to
`https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls` with that key, and session control +
transcripts flow over the `oai-events` data channel. The secret `OPENAI_API_KEY`
never reaches the client.

Keep `OPENAI_API_KEY` in **fnox** and run via `fnox exec -- bun run dev`. No
`OPENAI_*` values live in `.env` files.

Per-persona config (voice, multi-line instructions, opening line, reasoning
effort, turn-detection) lives in the typed module **`lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts`**
— a shared `BASE` (model / reasoning / `gpt-realtime-whisper` input transcription /
turn-detection) plus a per-persona map of OpenAI voice + prompt + greeting,
resolved by `resolveOpenaiAgent(personaId)`. The persona `instructions` follow a
light slice of OpenAI's Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton (Role, Personality & Tone,
Pacing, Unclear Audio, Variety).

Pick the **OPENAI** row under Providers (it's the default), choose a persona, and
press CALL — it mints a key, negotiates WebRTC, plays the agent's audio, shows the
user + agent transcripts (whisper for input), and barges in on server-VAD speech
detection. Without `OPENAI_API_KEY` set, CALL shows a clear "OPENAI_API_KEY is not
set" caption instead of connecting.

Multi-provider by design: the UI binds to a provider-agnostic session adapter.
Every provider row runs the mocked lifecycle except **ElevenLabs**, which is
wired to a real agent via `@elevenlabs/react`.

## Stack

- **Next.js** (App Router) · **React 19** · **Tailwind v4**
- **bun** package manager · **oxlint** + **oxfmt** (lint/format)
- **ElevenLabs UI** (shadcn-style, copied into `components/ui/`): `Orb` (WebGL,
  gradient style), `BarVisualizer` (soundbars), `MicSelector` (device picker)
- Hybrid orb: ElevenLabs WebGL orb for `gradient`; ported CSS/SVG orb for
  `mono` / `particles`

## Getting started

```bash
bun install
bun run dev        # http://localhost:3000
```

Or via **mise** tasks (load fnox secrets and give you a clean stop):

```bash
mise run dev       # = fnox exec -- bun run dev (ElevenLabs/xAI/OpenAI keys loaded)
mise run stop      # stop the server on PORT (default 3000)
```

Other scripts:

```bash
bun run lint       # oxlint
bun run fmt        # oxfmt (write)
bun run build      # production build
```

## Wiring the real ElevenLabs provider

Create `.env.local` (gitignored):

```bash
# Public agent: ID is enough. Private agents need a signed-URL token route.
NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID=your-agent-id
ELEVENLABS_API_KEY=your-api-key
```

Then pick the **ELEVENLABS** row under Providers and press CALL — it grants the
mic, streams a live transcript, and drives the orb/bars from real audio.

## Wiring the real xAI Grok provider

xAI's realtime API is **WebSocket-only** (no native browser WebRTC). The browser
connects directly to `wss://api.x.ai/v1/realtime`, authenticated by a short-lived
**ephemeral client-secret** minted server-side at `POST /api/xai/token` — the
secret `XAI_API_KEY` never reaches the client.

The only secret is the API key — keep it in **fnox** and run via
`fnox exec -- bun run dev`. No `XAI_*` values live in `.env` files.

Everything declarative (model, voice, multi-line instructions, opening line,
tools) lives in a typed config module — **`lib/realtime/xai-agent.ts`** — the way
ElevenLabs keeps each agent in `agent_configs/*.json`. It's a shared `BASE`
(model/tools/turn-detection) plus a **per-persona** map: each app persona
(`ARIA`/`ONYX`/`SAGE`/`NOVA`/`ECHO`/`CIPHER`) maps to a Grok voice + its own
prompt + greeting. The selected persona drives the live session via
`resolveXaiAgent(personaId)`. Edit that file to personalize — no env strings.

Pick the **XAI** row under Providers, choose a persona, and press CALL — it mints
a token, opens the WebSocket, captures the mic as PCM16, plays the agent's audio,
streams transcripts, and barges in on server-VAD speech detection. Without
`XAI_API_KEY` set, CALL shows a clear "XAI_API_KEY is not set" caption instead of
connecting.

## Wiring the real OpenAI provider

OpenAI's realtime API (`gpt-realtime-2`) connects over **WebRTC** — the browser's
peer connection carries the audio both ways, so there's no hand-rolled PCM
pipeline. A short-lived **ephemeral key** is minted server-side at
`POST /api/openai/token`; the browser then POSTs its SDP offer straight to
`https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls` with that key, and session control +
transcripts flow over the `oai-events` data channel. The secret `OPENAI_API_KEY`
never reaches the client.

Keep `OPENAI_API_KEY` in **fnox** and run via `fnox exec -- bun run dev`. No
`OPENAI_*` values live in `.env` files.

Per-persona config (voice, multi-line instructions, opening line, reasoning
effort, turn-detection) lives in the typed module **`lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts`**
— a shared `BASE` (model / reasoning / `gpt-realtime-whisper` input transcription /
turn-detection) plus a per-persona map of OpenAI voice + prompt + greeting,
resolved by `resolveOpenaiAgent(personaId)`. The persona `instructions` follow a
light slice of OpenAI's Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton (Role, Personality & Tone,
Pacing, Unclear Audio, Variety).

Pick the **OPENAI** row under Providers (it's the default), choose a persona, and
press CALL — it mints a key, negotiates WebRTC, plays the agent's audio, shows the
user + agent transcripts (whisper for input), and barges in on server-VAD speech
detection. Without `OPENAI_API_KEY` set, CALL shows a clear "OPENAI_API_KEY is not
set" caption instead of connecting.

## Architecture

```
app/                       layout (fonts), globals.css (brutalist + orb styles), page (ConversationProvider)
app/api/xai/token/         route handler that mints the xAI ephemeral client-secret
app/api/openai/token/      route handler that mints the OpenAI ephemeral key
components/ui/             ElevenLabs + shadcn components (copied, editable)
components/tsubaki/   app-shell (client boundary), top-bar, nav, the four views,
                           orb-visualizer (hybrid), custom-orb, bars, tools-button,
                           transcript-drawer, scroll-area, primitives, glyphs, tweaks-panel
hooks/                     use-tweaks (localStorage), use-media-query
lib/data.ts                personas, providers (with engine discriminator), tools, mock transcript
lib/realtime/              types (CallState, SessionApi), use-realtime-session (dispatcher),
                           use-xai-session (Grok WS engine), xai-audio (PCM16 + playback),
                           xai-agent (per-persona Grok config: voice + prompt + greeting)
```

provider is ElevenLabs; otherwise the mocked timers own the lifecycle.

Key architectural intent:
- The UI binds to a provider-agnostic `SessionApi` (`lib/realtime/`). Every provider row runs the **mock** lifecycle except **ElevenLabs**, which is wired to a real agent via `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` + `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID`.

Fixes/learnings from wiring it (all in `lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts`):
- `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` methods (`setMuted`, `getInputVolume`, `getOutputVolume`) **throw "No active conversation" if called before `startSession()`**. The mute effect was crashing the page the moment ELEVENLABS was selected. Guard `setMuted` on `status === "connected"`; wrap the volume getters in try/catch → return 0. The mock being the default provider is why this stayed latent.
- `livekit-client` is pinned to `2.16.1` via `package.json` `overrides` (skill-recommended WebRTC workaround); it already resolved there anyway.
- Agent IDs are **not secret** (public-widget embeddable). - List the user's agents: `fnox exec -- elevenlabs agents list`. All three (explorer / Travel guide / Japan Culture Expert) are `enable_auth:false` → connectable with agent ID alone, no signed-URL route.

description: Tsubaki (formerly Persona·Plex) realtime voice console — what it is and the pending work

This project is **Tsubaki** (renamed from **Persona·Plex** — 古椿の霊, the old-camellia-tree spirit; default accent is camellia crimson `#B0122F`, burnt orange still selectable), a brutalist/editorial multi-provider realtime voice console recreated from a Claude Design handoff bundle, built on Next.js (App Router) + bun + oxlint/oxfmt, using ElevenLabs UI primitives (`Orb`, `BarVisualizer`, `MicSelector`). The full internal rename landed: `components/tsubaki/`, CSS scope `.tsubaki`/`.tsubaki-dark`, var prefix `--tb-`, class prefix `tb-`.

Key architectural intent:
- The UI binds to a provider-agnostic `SessionApi` (`lib/realtime/`). `provider.engine` selects the engine: absent ⇒ **mock** lifecycle; `elevenlabs` ⇒ `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` + `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID`; `xai` ⇒ direct WebSocket (`use-xai-session` + `xai-audio` PCM16 + `/api/xai/token`); `openai` ⇒ **gpt-realtime-2 over WebRTC** (`use-openai-session` + `/api/openai/token`, ephemeral key → `POST /v1/realtime/calls`; WebRTC handles all audio, no PCM pipeline; input transcript via `gpt-realtime-whisper`). The two custom hooks share one interface; `use-realtime-session` picks the active one as `custom` and routes all controls through it.
- Per-persona config lives in typed modules: `lib/realtime/xai-agent.ts` (`resolveXaiAgent`) and `lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts` (`resolveOpenaiAgent`, OpenAI voices + `reasoningEffort` + light Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton).
- Hybrid orb: ElevenLabs WebGL orb for the `gradient` style; ported CSS/SVG orb for `mono`/`particles`. OpenAI orb levels come from Web Audio `AnalyserNode`s tapping the mic + remote WebRTC streams.

**Real provider status: VERIFIED working end-to-end** (was previously untested). Drove a live session against the user's public `explorer` agent — connect → token 200 → LiveKit WebRTC → live STT user turns + agent TTS in caption/transcript + orb reactivity → hang-up. Mock also fully verified.

Fixes/learnings from wiring it (all in `lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts`):
- `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` methods (`setMuted`, `getInputVolume`, `getOutputVolume`) **throw "No active conversation" if called before `startSession()`**. The mute effect was crashing the page the moment ELEVENLABS was selected. Guard `setMuted` on `status === "connected"`; wrap the volume getters in try/catch → return 0. The mock being the default provider is why this stayed latent.
- `livekit-client` is pinned to `2.16.1` via `package.json` `overrides` (skill-recommended WebRTC workaround); it already resolved there anyway.
- Agent IDs are **not secret** (public-widget embeddable). The user's key lives in **fnox**; for non-interactive shells use `fnox exec -- <cmd>` (the `fnox activate` zsh hook doesn't fire). `.env*` writes are blocked by a hook, so for a quick dev test export inline: `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID=<id> bun run dev` (persist via `.env.local` yourself).
- List the user's agents: `fnox exec -- elevenlabs agents list`. All three (explorer / Travel guide / Japan Culture Expert) are `enable_auth:false` → connectable with agent ID alone, no signed-URL route.

**How to apply:** consult [[elevenlabs-skills]] (`agents` + `setup-api-key`) before changing the integration.

content.text:
Implementation complete. All four gates pass (`tsc --noEmit` → `lint` → `fmt:check` → `build`), and the `/api/openai/token` route is registered in the build.

## What landed

**New files**
- [app/api/openai/token/route.ts](app/api/openai/token/route.ts) — mints an ephemeral key via `POST /v1/realtime/client_secrets` (clone of the xAI route, OpenAI-pointed).
- [lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts](lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts) — `resolveOpenaiAgent(personaId)`; the 6 personas re-mapped to OpenAI voices (marin/cedar/sage/coral/echo/ballad), `reasoningEffort` (default `low`), `gpt-realtime-whisper` input transcription, and per-persona `instructions` lightly structured to OpenAI's Realtime 2.0 skeleton (Role / Personality & Tone / Pacing / Unclear Audio / Variety).
- [lib/realtime/use-openai-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-openai-session.ts) — the WebRTC engine. `getUserMedia` → `RTCPeerConnection` → `oai-events` data channel → ephemeral key → `POST /v1/realtime/calls` SDP exchange. WebRTC carries audio both ways (no PCM pipeline); `session.update` sets voice/instructions/whisper/`reasoning.effort` before the greeting; orb levels come from Web Audio `AnalyserNode`s on the mic + remote streams; barge-in via server VAD (+ `response.cancel`/`output_audio_buffer.clear` on manual interrupt).

**Edited**
- [lib/data.ts](lib/data.ts) — `engine` union gains `"openai"`; the default OPENAI provider row now has `engine: "openai"`.
- [lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts) — generalized the old `isXai` ternaries into a single `custom = xai | openai | null` dispatch; both hooks called unconditionally.
- [README.md](README.md) — new "Wiring the real OpenAI provider" section + architecture map.

## The one remaining step (yours)

`OPENAI_API_KEY` isn't in fnox yet. Add to [fnox.toml](fnox.toml):

```toml
[providers.openai]
type = "keychain"
service = "fnox"          # or "openai" — match how you store it

[secrets]
OPENAI_API_KEY = REDACTED provider = "openai", value = "OPENAI_API_KEY" }
```

…then store the key in the keychain. After that:

```bash
mise run dev     # = fnox exec -- bun run dev
```

Select **OPENAI** (it's the default row) → pick a persona → **CALL**. Expect: `POST /api/openai/token` → 200 with a `value`, then `POST .../v1/realtime/calls` → 200 SDP; the persona greeting plays, your speech shows as user turns (whisper), and talking over the agent triggers barge-in. Without the key, CALL shows a clear "OPENAI_API_KEY is not set" caption rather than failing silently.

One thing to flag honestly: I verified the code (types/lint/format/build) but **not a live call** — that needs the key and a mic, so the runtime behavior of the session shape against the real API is still unconfirmed. If anything mismatches at runtime (e.g. an event name or the `reasoning.effort` nesting), it'll surface as an `error` caption and I can adjust.

This project is **Tsubaki** (renamed from **Persona·Plex** — 古椿の霊, the old-camellia-tree spirit; default accent is camellia crimson `#B0122F`, burnt orange still selectable), a brutalist/editorial multi-provider realtime voice console recreated from a Claude Design handoff bundle, built on Next.js (App Router) + bun + oxlint/oxfmt, using ElevenLabs UI primitives (`Orb`, `BarVisualizer`, `MicSelector`). The full internal rename landed: `components/tsubaki/`, CSS scope `.tsubaki`/`.tsubaki-dark`, var prefix `--tb-`, class prefix `tb-`.

Key architectural intent:
- The UI binds to a provider-agnostic `SessionApi` (`lib/realtime/`). `provider.engine` selects the engine: absent ⇒ **mock** lifecycle; `elevenlabs` ⇒ `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` + `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID`; `xai` ⇒ direct WebSocket (`use-xai-session` + `xai-audio` PCM16 + `/api/xai/token`); `openai` ⇒ **gpt-realtime-2 over WebRTC** (`use-openai-session` + `/api/openai/token`, ephemeral key → `POST /v1/realtime/calls`; WebRTC handles all audio, no PCM pipeline; input transcript via `gpt-realtime-whisper`). The two custom hooks share one interface; `use-realtime-session` picks the active one as `custom` and routes all controls through it.
- Per-persona config lives in typed modules: `lib/realtime/xai-agent.ts` (`resolveXaiAgent`) and `lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts` (`resolveOpenaiAgent`, OpenAI voices + `reasoningEffort` + light Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton).

Mock also fully verified.

Fixes/learnings from wiring it (all in `lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts`):
- `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` methods (`setMuted`, `getInputVolume`, `getOutputVolume`) **throw "No active conversation" if called before `startSession()`**. The mute effect was crashing the page the moment ELEVENLABS was selected. Guard `setMuted` on `status === "connected"`; wrap the volume getters in try/catch → return 0. The mock being the default provider is why this stayed latent.
- `livekit-client` is pinned to `2.16.1` via `package.json` `overrides` (skill-recommended WebRTC workaround); it already resolved there anyway.
- Agent IDs are **not secret** (public-widget embeddable). ---
name: strictmode-pure-setstate-updaters
description: setState updater functions must be pure — StrictMode double-invokes them, silently dropping turns if they mutate refs
metadata:
  type: project
---

In the realtime session hooks (`lib/realtime/use-xai-session.ts`, `use-openai-session.ts`), the `setTurns((prev) => …)` updater functions **must be pure** — no mutating refs (`agentTurnIdRef.current = …`, `turnSeqRef.current++`) inside the updater.

**Why:** Next dev defaults to `reactStrictMode: true`, which **double-invokes state updater functions** to surface impurity. An impure updater that sets `agentTurnIdRef.current = newId` on the first invocation makes the second invocation take the `prev.map(...)` no-op branch on an empty array, so the new transcript turn is discarded. Symptom seen 2026-06-07: OpenAI engine connected fine and `setCaption`/`setCallState` (pure value updates) worked, but the transcript drawer stayed at "0 TURNS" while captions streamed — because only the `setTurns` updater was impure. Both hooks had the same latent bug; xAI's was hidden because its drawer turns weren't closely checked.

**How to apply:** compute the id / sequence number and mutate the ref **before** calling `setTurns`, then pass a pure updater that only reads `prev` and the captured values. Verify transcript turns actually render in the drawer (not just the live `callState === "speaking"` placeholder block in [[realtime-persona-overview]]'s transcript-drawer) before declaring a voice engine done.

content.text:
Verified end-to-end in Chrome, with one real bug found and fixed along the way.

## What the live test showed

Driving the app with chrome-devtools MCP (1440×900, real mic, permission granted):

- **Token + WebRTC handshake:** `POST /api/openai/token` → **200** (returns `ek_…`, confirms `gpt-realtime-2`), then `POST https://api.openai.com/v1/realtime/calls` → **201**.
- **Session config applied:** ARIA greeted **in-character** — *"Hi, I'm Aria, and I'm glad you're here…"* — proving `session.update` pushed the persona voice + instructions before first audio.
- **Event stream (instrumented the `oai-events` channel):** `session.created`/`updated`, 133 `response.output_audio_transcript.delta`, `response.done`, plus `input_audio_buffer.speech_started`×4 and `conversation.item.truncated`×2 (barge-in working), and `conversation.item.input_audio_transcription.delta`/`.completed` (whisper user transcripts arriving).
- **Mute** (no barge-in while muted) and **clean teardown** on hang-up (→ ENDED → "Call") both confirmed.
- Console clean except a pre-existing THREE.js deprecation warning.

## The bug I found and fixed

The transcript drawer stayed at **"0 TURNS"** even though captions streamed. Root cause: my `setTurns((prev) => …)` updaters **mutated refs inside the updater** (`agentTurnIdRef.current = newId`, `turnSeqRef.current++`). Next dev runs **React StrictMode**, which **double-invokes state updaters** to surface impurity — the second invocation saw the already-set ref and took the `prev.map` no-op branch on an empty array, discarding every new turn. `setCaption`/`setCallState` use plain values, so they were unaffected — which is why caption updated but turns didn't.

Fix: made the updaters pure (compute id / bump the sequence *before* `setTurns`, pass an updater that only reads `prev`). After the fix the drawer correctly shows **"1 TURNS"** with the agent greeting rendered. I applied the same fix to [use-xai-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-xai-session.ts) — it had the identical latent bug ([use-openai-session.ts](lib/realtime/use-openai-session.ts) was the one under test).

All four gates re-pass after the changes: `tsc` → `lint` → `fmt:check` → `build`.

## One thing I couldn't fully exercise

User-turn *rendering* — the room was quiet during the unmuted window, so no clean user turn was produced live. But the user-transcription **events did arrive** (instrumented run) and they render through the exact same pure-updater path I just verified for agent turns, so I'm confident in it; if you speak during a call you should see "YOU" turns appear.

The dev server is still running in the background (started via `fnox exec -- bun run dev`). Stop it with `mise run stop` when you're done, or keep testing other personas.

Voice activity detection (VAD) is a feature available in the Realtime API allowing to automatically detect when the user has started or stopped speaking.
It is enabled by default in [speech-to-speech](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations) Realtime sessions, but is optional and can be turned off.
In [transcription](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-transcription) Realtime sessions, turn detection support depends on the transcription model. Models that support VAD default to `server_vad`, while `gpt-realtime-whisper` requires turn detection to be omitted or set to `null`.

## Overview

When VAD is enabled, the audio is chunked automatically and the Realtime API sends events to indicate when the user has started or stopped speaking:

- `input_audio_buffer.speech_started`: The start of a speech turn
- `input_audio_buffer.speech_stopped`: The end of a speech turn

You can use these events to handle speech turns in your application. For example, you can use them to manage conversation state or process transcripts in chunks.

You can configure VAD with the [`session.update`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/api-reference/realtime-client-events/session/update) client event by setting `session.audio.input.turn_detection`.

There are two modes for VAD:

- `server_vad`: Automatically chunks the audio based on periods of silence.
- `semantic_vad`: Chunks the audio when the model believes based on the words said by the user that they have completed their utterance.

For sessions and models that support VAD, the default value is `server_vad`.

Read below to learn more about the different modes.

## Server VAD

Server VAD is the default mode for speech-to-speech sessions, and for transcription sessions on models that support turn detection. It uses periods of silence to automatically chunk the audio.

You can adjust the following properties to fine-tune the VAD settings:

- `threshold`: Activation threshold (0 to 1). A higher threshold will require louder audio to activate the model, and thus might perform better in noisy environments.
- `prefix_padding_ms`: Amount of audio (in milliseconds) to include before the VAD detected speech.
- `silence_duration_ms`: Duration of silence (in milliseconds) to detect speech stop. With shorter values turns will be detected more quickly.

Voice activity detection (VAD) is a feature available in the Realtime API allowing to automatically detect when the user has started or stopped speaking.
It is enabled by default in [speech-to-speech](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-conversations) Realtime sessions, but is optional and can be turned off.
In [transcription](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/realtime-transcription) Realtime sessions, turn detection support depends on the transcription model. Models that support VAD default to `server_vad`, while `gpt-realtime-whisper` requires turn detection to be omitted or set to `null`.

## Overview

When VAD is enabled, the audio is chunked automatically and the Realtime API sends events to indicate when the user has started or stopped speaking:

- `input_audio_buffer.speech_started`: The start of a speech turn
- `input_audio_buffer.speech_stopped`: The end of a speech turn

You can use these events to handle speech turns in your application. For example, you can use them to manage conversation state or process transcripts in chunks.

You can configure VAD with the [`session.update`](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/api-reference/realtime-client-events/session/update) client event by setting `session.audio.input.turn_detection`.

There are two modes for VAD:

- `server_vad`: Automatically chunks the audio based on periods of silence.
- `semantic_vad`: Chunks the audio when the model believes based on the words said by the user that they have completed their utterance.

For sessions and models that support VAD, the default value is `server_vad`.

Read below to learn more about the different modes.

## Server VAD

Server VAD is the default mode for speech-to-speech sessions, and for transcription sessions on models that support turn detection. It uses periods of silence to automatically chunk the audio.

You can adjust the following properties to fine-tune the VAD settings:

- `threshold`: Activation threshold (0 to 1). A higher threshold will require louder audio to activate the model, and thus might perform better in noisy environments.
- `prefix_padding_ms`: Amount of audio (in milliseconds) to include before the VAD detected speech.
- `silence_duration_ms`: Duration of silence (in milliseconds) to detect speech stop. With shorter values turns will be detected more quickly.

```
          "threshold": 0.5,
          "prefix_padding_ms": 300,
          "silence_duration_ms": 500,
          "create_response": true, // only in conversation mode
          "interrupt_response": true // only in conversation mode
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
```

content.text:
I've reviewed the VAD guide against our implementation. Here's the finding:

## What we currently send

We **always** send `session.audio.input.turn_detection` as a tuned `server_vad` object — we never set it to `null` or omit it. That part is correct: for a hands-free conversational agent you *want* VAD on (null/omit means manual push-to-talk + `input_audio_buffer.commit`, which isn't this UX). So the structure is right; the problem is **tuning** and a **gap in what we expose**.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- **`threshold` is the sensitivity lever** (0–1): *"A higher threshold will require louder audio to activate… might perform better in noisy environments."* Our presets sit at **0.4–0.6** (SNAPPY 0.6 / RELAXED 0.5 / PATIENT 0.4) — at or below OpenAI's 0.5 default, i.e. on the sensitive side. This matches what we saw in testing: ARIA kept reacting to ambient room noise.
- **`semantic_vad`** is OpenAI's purpose-built answer to over-triggering: it chunks on whether the user *semantically* finished a thought, so it's *"less likely to interrupt the user"* and ignores stray noise/fillers. Tuned via `eagerness` (low/medium/high/auto), not `threshold`.
- **Gap in our config type:** `OpenaiAgentConfig.turnDetection` only models `threshold`/`silence_duration_ms`/`prefix_padding_ms`. It can't express `eagerness`, `create_response`, or `interrupt_response` — so semantic VAD isn't actually configurable yet even though the `type` union allows it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

So: not a null/omit bug — a sensitivity-tuning choice. There are two good ways to fix it, with different feel:

questions.question: How should we reduce the input sensitivity for the OpenAI engine's turn detection?

options.label: Switch to semantic_vad (recommended)
options.description: Use type: "semantic_vad" with eagerness mapped per persona (low for ARIA/ECHO/CIPHER so they let you finish; medium for SAGE/NOVA). OpenAI's purpose-built fix for over-triggering — chunks on whether you've semantically finished speaking, so background noise and fillers don't fire a turn. Less 'it jumped in on me' feel. eagerness replaces threshold.

options.label: Raise server_vad thresholds
options.description: Keep energy-based server_vad but make it much less sensitive: e.g. SNAPPY 0.7 / RELAXED 0.8 / PATIENT 0.9, optionally longer silence_duration_ms. Predictable, simple, and exactly the doc's noisy-environment guidance. Keeps the current barge-in feel, just harder to trigger on noise.

options.label: Hybrid per persona
options.description: semantic_vad (eagerness low) for the slow/atmospheric personas (ARIA/ECHO/CIPHER) and higher-threshold server_vad for the snappy ones (SAGE/NOVA). Most tailored, but more moving parts to reason about and test.

This project is **Tsubaki** (renamed from **Persona·Plex** — 古椿の霊, the old-camellia-tree spirit; default accent is camellia crimson `#B0122F`, burnt orange still selectable), a brutalist/editorial multi-provider realtime voice console recreated from a Claude Design handoff bundle, built on Next.js (App Router) + bun + oxlint/oxfmt, using ElevenLabs UI primitives (`Orb`, `BarVisualizer`, `MicSelector`). The full internal rename landed: `components/tsubaki/`, CSS scope `.tsubaki`/`.tsubaki-dark`, var prefix `--tb-`, class prefix `tb-`.

Key architectural intent:
- The UI binds to a provider-agnostic `SessionApi` (`lib/realtime/`). `provider.engine` selects the engine: absent ⇒ **mock** lifecycle; `elevenlabs` ⇒ `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` + `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID`; `xai` ⇒ direct WebSocket (`use-xai-session` + `xai-audio` PCM16 + `/api/xai/token`); `openai` ⇒ **gpt-realtime-2 over WebRTC** (`use-openai-session` + `/api/openai/token`, ephemeral key → `POST /v1/realtime/calls`; WebRTC handles all audio, no PCM pipeline; input transcript via `gpt-realtime-whisper`). The two custom hooks share one interface; `use-realtime-session` picks the active one as `custom` and routes all controls through it.
- Per-persona config lives in typed modules: `lib/realtime/xai-agent.ts` (`resolveXaiAgent`) and `lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts` (`resolveOpenaiAgent`, OpenAI voices + `reasoningEffort` + light Realtime 2.0 prompt skeleton).
- Hybrid orb: ElevenLabs WebGL orb for the `gradient` style; ported CSS/SVG orb for `mono`/`particles`. OpenAI orb levels come from Web Audio `AnalyserNode`s tapping the mic + remote WebRTC streams.

**Real provider status:** ElevenLabs **VERIFIED working end-to-end** — live session against the user's public `explorer` agent (connect → token 200 → LiveKit WebRTC → live STT/TTS + orb → hang-up). xAI Grok integration landed (on `main`). OpenAI `gpt-realtime-2` (WebRTC) integration landed on branch `feat/gpt-voice-agent` and is **VERIFIED working end-to-end** in Chrome (chrome-devtools MCP): `/api/openai/token` 200 → `POST /v1/realtime/calls` 201 → data channel → `session.update` applied the persona voice+instructions (ARIA greeted warmly in-character) → agent transcript streamed into caption + drawer turns → barge-in/VAD events + user-input whisper transcription events flow → clean hang-up teardown. `OPENAI_API_KEY` is now in fnox. Mock also fully verified.

Fixes/learnings from wiring it (all in `lib/realtime/use-realtime-session.ts`):
- `@elevenlabs/react` `useConversation` methods (`setMuted`, `getInputVolume`, `getOutputVolume`) **throw "No active conversation" if called before `startSession()`**. The mute effect was crashing the page the moment ELEVENLABS was selected. Guard `setMuted` on `status === "connected"`; wrap the volume getters in try/catch → return 0. The mock being the default provider is why this stayed latent.
- `livekit-client` is pinned to `2.16.1` via `package.json` `overrides` (skill-recommended WebRTC workaround); it already resolved there anyway.
- Agent IDs are **not secret** (public-widget embeddable). The user's key lives in **fnox**; for non-interactive shells use `fnox exec -- <cmd>` (the `fnox activate` zsh hook doesn't fire). `.env*` writes are blocked by a hook, so for a quick dev test export inline: `NEXT_PUBLIC_ELEVENLABS_AGENT_ID=<id> bun run dev` (persist via `.env.local` yourself).
- List the user's agents: `fnox exec -- elevenlabs agents list`. All three (explorer / Travel guide / Japan Culture Expert) are `enable_auth:false` → connectable with agent ID alone, no signed-URL route.

**How to apply:** consult [[elevenlabs-skills]] (`agents` + `setup-api-key`) before changing the integration.

content.text:
Done. Here's the review and what changed.

## Answer to your question
No — we were **not** setting `turn_detection` to `null` or omitting it. We always sent a `server_vad` object, which is the *correct* posture for a hands-free conversational agent (null/omit means manual push-to-talk + `input_audio_buffer.commit`). The "too sensitive" symptom was a **tuning** problem, not a missing-config problem:

- Our `server_vad` thresholds were **0.4–0.6** — at/below OpenAI's 0.5 default, so room noise kept tripping turn detection (exactly the "ARIA keeps reacting to ambient noise" behavior we saw in testing).
- A real gap: the `turnDetection` **type couldn't even express** `eagerness` / `create_response` / `interrupt_response`, so `semantic_vad` wasn't actually configurable despite the `type` union allowing it.

## What I changed (per your choice: semantic_vad)
In [lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts](lib/realtime/openai-agent.ts):
- Added a `VadEagerness` type and **extended** `turnDetection` to fully model both modes: `eagerness` (semantic), `threshold`/`silence_duration_ms`/`prefix_padding_ms` (server), plus `create_response`/`interrupt_response`.
- Converted the three presets to `semantic_vad`, mapping pacing → eagerness: **`low`** for ARIA/ONYX/ECHO/CIPHER (let them finish), **`medium`** for SAGE/NOVA. Updated the stale per-persona comments.

`use-openai-session.ts` already forwards `agent.turnDetection` straight into `session.audio.input.turn_detection`, so no hook change was needed.

## Verified live in Chrome
- Outgoing `session.update` now carries `turn_detection: { type: "semantic_vad", eagerness: "low" }` (ARIA).
- **OpenAI accepted it — zero error events** (confirms the field/shape is valid), `session.updated` received.
- Sensitivity dropped sharply: **1** `input_audio_buffer.speech_started` in 8 unmuted seconds vs **4** in the earlier energy-VAD run. Agent transcript still streams normally; clean hang-up.
- All four gates pass (`tsc` → `lint` → `fmt:check` → `build`).

Semantic VAD waits on *utterance completion* rather than raw loudness, so noise and "ummm…" fillers no longer trigger a turn. If any persona still feels too eager or too laggy, the single knob to turn is its `eagerness` (`low` ↔ `medium` ↔ `high`) in the presets — and `server_vad` with a higher `threshold` remains available in the type if you ever want to A/B it.

Note: the dev server is still running in the background — `mise run stop` when you're done.
